questions.q: Which function should you use to parse JSON from a string you already have in memory (not a file)?
options: json.load()
json.loads()
json.dump()
json.read()
questions.explain: json.loads() ("load string") parses JSON text held in a Python string. json.load() reads from an open file object instead.

questions.q: After parsing a JSON object with json.load(), what Python type does it become?
options: A tuple
A string
A dict
A custom JSONObject class
questions.explain: JSON objects map directly onto Python dicts, and JSON arrays map onto Python lists.

questions.q: A shipment record is missing the 'tracking_url' key. What happens if your script does response["tracking_url"] directly?
options: It silently returns None
It raises a KeyError, which can crash the whole batch job
It automatically returns an empty string
Python inserts the missing key with a default value
questions.explain: Direct dict-key lookup raises a KeyError when the key is absent. In a batch job, that one bad record can stop the entire run unless you handle it.

questions.q: What does response.get("tracking_url", "not available") do if the key is missing?
options: Raises a KeyError anyway
Returns the string "not available" instead of crashing
Adds the key to the dict permanently
Returns None regardless of the default given
questions.explain: dict.get(key, default) returns the given default when the key isn't present, instead of raising an exception.

questions.q: What does passing indent=2 to json.dump() or json.dumps() do?
options: It compresses the JSON to save space
It validates the JSON against a schema
It pretty-prints the output with 2-space nested indentation for readability
It converts the output to YAML instead
questions.explain: indent=2 formats the JSON output with readable nested indentation, which is useful for logs or files a human will read, at the cost of a larger output size.
